**Text B: The Architecture of Connection**

For most of human history, people did not choose their neighbours. They were born into communities — villages, neighbourhoods, extended families — where social contact was unavoidable rather than optional. Historians and sociologists increasingly argue that this enforced togetherness, uncomfortable as it sometimes was, built the social muscles that modern urban life has allowed to atrophy.

The good news, according to researchers at University College London, is that environments shape behaviour. When people cannot avoid each other — in a well-designed courtyard, a shared laundry room, or a slow lift — they tend to talk. Small talk leads to familiarity; familiarity reduces fear; reduced fear opens the door to genuine trust. The design of a building is, in this sense, a social policy.

This insight has influenced a wave of new housing projects across Northern Europe. In co-housing developments in Denmark and the Netherlands, residents typically have small private apartments but share kitchens, workshops, and gardens. Studies following residents over time report significantly lower rates of loneliness and higher satisfaction with daily life compared with equivalent populations in conventional housing. Critically, residents did not choose co-housing because they were already sociable people; many were shy or sceptical at first. The environment changed their behaviour.

Critics point out that co-housing remains expensive and available only to those who can afford it or who are lucky enough to enter a state-subsidised scheme. Social infrastructure, they warn, must not become another privilege of the affluent. The challenge, then, is to export the lessons of the co-housing courtyard into everyday urban design — bus shelters wide enough to have a conversation, benches that face each other, stairwells lit and decorated well enough that people do not rush through them.
